entry.summary:
Source: @bijanabdolkarimi

Civilizational Iranian-Islamic Intellectualism ✍️ Seyyed Mohammad Javad Bani Saeed Langeroudi. Intellectualism in Iran after the Islamic Revolution is not merely faced with the issue of critiquing tradition or adapting and localizing new theories; rather, the more fundamental issue is the possibility of the formation of "Iranian-Islamic civilizational intellectualism": an intellectualism that can create a coherent, rational, and path-opening system in the relationship between truth and reality, revelation and reason, identity and progress, heritage and future, and historical belonging and social responsibility. This article, with a conceptual, normative, and civilizational approach, addresses the formulation of the model of the civilizational intellectual. Its main claim is that this model is neither limited to imitating dominant global concepts and theoretical frameworks, nor is it reduced to an uncritical defense of the past and tradition, nor does it see its function as justifying the status quo; rather, it is an epistemic, moral, and social activism that, relying on revelatory sources, demonstrative rationality, the historical experience of Iran and Islam, and a precise understanding of contemporary issues and developments, seeks to produce concepts, theorize, and open the civilizational horizon of society. Civilizational intellectualism is truth-oriented and independent in knowledge; it understands religion as a system with explanatory capacity and social orientation; it reconciles critique and defense, loyalty and reform, and idealism and realism; and it regards critique not merely as negation and denial, but as a prelude to establishment, offering alternatives, and institution-building. Epistemic independence, conscious historical belonging, conceptual production, problem-orientation, foundational critique, responsible presence in the public sphere, the ability to combine rationality and spirituality, and attention to education and institution-building are among the fundamental components of this model. At the end, the article examines the epistemic, educational, and institutional requirements for the realization of such intellectualism. 🔗 Read the full note @bijanabdolkarimi

entry.summary:
Source: @bijanabdolkarimi

The Crisis of Self-Defeating and Short-Sighted Intellectualism ✍️ Seyyed Mohammad Javad Bani Saeed Langeroudi

Decades after the victory of Iran's Islamic Revolution, one of the fundamental questions in the realm of social and cultural thought is: what relationship have intellectual elites and so-called intellectual currents established with the reconstruction of the national and religious identity of Iranian society? The historical expectation of the Iranian Muslim intellectual was that, in the face of the extensive epistemological, media, civilizational, and lifestyle onslaught of opposing currents, they would creatively revisit the heritage of Iran, Islam, and Islamic-Iranian civilization, and provide a new apparatus for its defense, explanation, and extension. However, in a significant portion of this current, instead of such a mission, one observes a kind of theoretical passivity, infatuation with modernity and postmodernity, distrust of indigenous heritage, and even alignment with aggressive discourses. This article, with a critical approach, examines the identity crisis of dependent intellectualism, its inability to formulate a new Iranian-Islamic identity, and the cultural, legal, economic, and social consequences of this inefficiency.

📚 Journalism of War and Peace | Author: Abdolreza Aalami | First Edition | Naqd-e Farhang Publications | 2026 | In a world where every armed conflict is narrated on news pages and in cyberspace before it is decided on the battlefield, this is the fundamental question: What responsibility does a journalist have? This book examines two distinct approaches to media coverage of conflicts: war journalism, which focuses on violence, dramatization, and winner-loser narratives, and peace journalism, which places the roots of conflict, hidden voices, and ways out at the center of attention. These two approaches not only define the method of reporting but also influence public opinion, political decisions, and even the course of conflicts. Drawing on the theories of Johan Galtung, the founder of the concept of peace journalism, and the views of Jake Lynch and Annabel McGoldrick, this book blends theory with field experience. Case studies from Gaza, Ukraine, Syria, and Sudan show how editorial choices, from camera angle to source selection, can make war seem natural or peace possible. The book also addresses the new challenges of journalism in the digital age: cyber warfare, misinformation, and cyberspace as a parallel battlefield whose rules are still being formed. This book is written for journalism and communications students, field journalists, and any curious reader who wants to understand how the media narrate war—and what that narration costs. The media is not a mirror of reality, but its constructor. 🛒Click on this link to buy the book🛒🟠Join Naqd-e Farhang on Instagram🟠@naqdefarhangpub.
